claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has higher plastic strain at failure than commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater toughness than commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading.
Severe lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr contributes to its higher plastic strain and toughness.
Solid-solution strengthening from the multielement composition contributes to higher plastic strain and toughness in WTaTiVZr.
The equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy possesses severe lattice distortion and a multielement solid-solution structure.
Pure tungsten has a comparatively simple BCC lattice.
The refractory elements in the WTaTiVZr alloy are randomly distributed.
The random elemental distribution in WTaTiVZr creates local lattice distortions.
The WTaTiVZr alloy contains a high density of atomic-scale obstacles to dislocation motion.
Atomic-scale obstacles in WTaTiVZr impede dislocation motion more effectively than the lattice of pure tungsten.
Greater impediment to dislocation motion in WTaTiVZr produces enhanced strain hardening.
Enhanced strain hardening allows WTaTiVZr to accommodate more plastic deformation before fracture.
Commercially used pure tungsten typically has limited ductility at high temperature.
Commercially used pure tungsten typically has low toughness at high temperature.
The limited ductility and low toughness of pure tungsten arise from its simple lattice and lack of solid-solution strengthening.
The range 800–1200 °C is relevant to sustained plasma-facing-component service.
The proposed effect may depend on grain size and phase stability.
Matched-grain-size WTaTiVZr and pure-tungsten specimens will be compared by tensile and Charpy impact testing at 1000 °C in an inert atmosphere.
Failure of WTaTiVZr to show higher plastic strain and impact energy than pure tungsten under the controlled test is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions call for strain rates typical of sustained service, whereas a Charpy impact test inherently applies rapid impact loading; the two loading regimes are not equivalent.
